text: What was the principal target of the 'Health for All' strategy outlined in the 1978 Alma-Ata Declaration?

options.A: To eradicate all genetic diseases from the world by the year 2020
options.B: To achieve a level of health that permits all people to lead socially and economically productive lives by the year 2000
options.C: To build a tertiary referral hospital in every town in developing countries
options.D: To ensure free medical surgery for all children under five globally

explanation: The principal target of 'Health for All by the Year 2000' was to achieve a level of health that would enable all citizens of the world to lead socially and economically productive lives through primary healthcare.

text: Which clinical indicators are used under IMCI guidelines to classify a child under five as having Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM)?

options.A: Weight-for-age below the median and skin rash
options.B: MUAC of less than 11.5 cm or presence of bilateral pitting pedal edema
options.C: Height-for-age below the median and dry skin
options.D: A bulging fontanelle and high fever

explanation: A child aged 6-59 months is diagnosed with Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) if they have a Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) of less than 11.5 cm, OR have bilateral pitting pedal edema (signs of kwashiorkor), or are severely wasted.

text: What is the difference between Antepartum Hemorrhage (APH) and Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH)?

options.A: APH is bleeding from the birth canal before 12 weeks of pregnancy; PPH is bleeding after 24 weeks
options.B: APH is bleeding from the birth canal from 28 weeks of pregnancy until the birth of the baby; PPH is bleeding of 500ml or more after delivery
options.C: APH is bleeding from the nose during pregnancy; PPH is bleeding from the uterus
options.D: APH occurs only in primigravida mothers; PPH occurs only in multigravida mothers

explanation: Antepartum Hemorrhage (APH) is bleeding from or into the genital tract after 28 weeks of gestation up to the delivery of the baby. Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH) is the loss of 500 ml or more of blood (or 1000 ml for cesarean) from the genital tract after childbirth.

text: What is the physiological significance of the Vaccine Vial Monitor (VVM) on a vaccine vial?

options.A: It measures the volume of vaccine left in the vial
options.B: It is a chemical indicator that changes color to show cumulative exposure to heat over time
options.C: It measures the expiry date of the glass vial material
options.D: It detects bacterial contamination inside the vaccine suspension

explanation: The VVM is a heat-sensitive label placed on vaccine vials. It changes color gradually when exposed to heat, reflecting cumulative heat exposure and indicating whether the vaccine has exceeded its safe limit.

text: In tuberculosis management, what is the primary purpose of the Directly Observed Treatment Short-course (DOTS) strategy?

options.A: To isolate patients in sanatoriums until they are cured
options.B: To ensure patients swallow their prescribed anti-TB medications under the direct observation of a health worker or trained supervisor
options.C: To provide free food supplements to patients' families
options.D: To verify the diagnosis of TB using chest X-rays monthly

explanation: The DOTS strategy requires a trained health worker or community treatment partner to directly observe the patient swallowing each dose of medication. This ensures treatment compliance, prevents default, and halts the development of drug-resistant tuberculosis.

text: Which of the following describes the core principle of community mobilization in primary healthcare?

options.A: Giving orders to community members about health behaviors
options.B: Empowering community members to identify their own health needs, plan, and take action to solve them
options.C: Paying community members cash to attend clinic services
options.D: Building large private clinics funded by external donor agencies

explanation: Community mobilization is a capacity-building process through which community individuals, groups, or organizations plan, carry out, and evaluate activities on a participatory basis to improve their health and sanitation.

text: What clinical triad characterizes pre-eclampsia in a pregnant woman?

options.A: Fever, vaginal discharge, and lower abdominal pain
options.B: New-onset hypertension after 20 weeks of gestation, proteinuria, and/or maternal organ dysfunction
options.C: Hypotension, bradycardia, and skin rash
options.D: Glycosuria, polyuria, and lifestyle indicators

explanation: Pre-eclampsia is a multi-system pregnancy disorder characterized by new-onset hypertension (BP >= 140/90 mmHg) presenting after 20 weeks of gestation, accompanied by significant protein in the urine (proteinuria) or other organ dysfunctions.

text: What is the primary danger of severe dehydration caused by acute watery diarrhea in a child?

options.A: Chronic vitamin deficiency
options.B: Loss of body water and essential electrolytes leading to hypovolemic shock and death
options.C: Destruction of intestinal microflora permanently
options.D: Development of chronic respiratory failure

explanation: Watery diarrhea causes rapid loss of fluids and key electrolytes (sodium, potassium, bicarbonate). If not replaced, it leads to severe hypovolemia, decreased tissue perfusion, organ failure, hypovolemic shock, and death.

text: Within what maximum timeframe should Emergency Contraceptive Pills (ECPs) be taken after unprotected sexual intercourse to be effective?

options.A: Within 24 hours only
options.B: Within 72 to 120 hours (3 to 5 days) depending on the type of pill
options.C: Within 2 weeks
options.D: Only after the first missed menstrual period

explanation: Emergency contraceptive pills (such as Levonorgestrel or Ulipristal Acetate) are most effective the sooner they are taken. Levonorgestrel is effective up to 72 hours (3 days), while Ulipristal acetate is effective up to 120 hours (5 days).

text: Why is an unconscious, breathing casualty placed in the recovery position during first aid?

options.A: To reduce blood flow to the brain and prevent fits
options.B: To keep the airway open, prevent the tongue from falling back, and allow fluids to drain from the mouth
options.C: To keep the body warm during hypothermia
options.D: To facilitate chest compressions if they stop breathing

explanation: The recovery position is a lateral recumbent position that uses gravity to keep the tongue from blocking the epiglottis. It also allows vomit or saliva to drain freely, preventing pulmonary aspiration.

text: Why must used needles never be recapped before disposal in a safety box?

options.A: It compromises the sterility of the needle for future use
options.B: Recapping is the leading cause of accidental needle-stick injuries among health workers, risking transmission of blood-borne pathogens
options.C: The plastic cap makes the safety box fill up too quickly
options.D: It prevents the needle from melting during incineration

explanation: Recapping needles using two hands poses a high risk of the needle slipping and puncturing the worker's finger. This exposes them to pathogens like HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C. Always drop needles directly into the safety box.

text: In disease surveillance, what is the meaning of an 'alert threshold' for an epidemic-prone disease?

options.A: The point at which all clinics in the country are shut down
options.B: The level of disease occurrence or single case that triggers an immediate investigation and preliminary active response
options.C: The maximum number of deaths allowed before reporting
options.D: The percentage of vaccine coverage in the community

explanation: An alert threshold is the pre-defined number of cases (sometimes a single case of a highly dangerous disease like cholera, yellow fever, or Lassa fever) that warns health authorities to investigate, collect samples, and prepare for a potential outbreak.

text: What is the primary rationale for administering Tetanus Toxoid (TT) or Tetanus-Diphtheria (Td) vaccine to pregnant women?

options.A: To protect the mother from wound infections during gardening
options.B: To allow the mother to pass protective antibodies to the fetus, preventing neonatal tetanus after birth
options.C: To prevent congenital malformations in the early fetus
options.D: To reduce the risk of maternal malaria infection

explanation: Vaccinating pregnant women with Tetanus Toxoid stimulates maternal IgG antibodies, which cross the placenta to the fetus. This passive immunity protects the newborn from neonatal tetanus, a fatal infection that can occur via an unsterile umbilical cord cut.

text: Under IMCI guidelines, why is oral zinc supplementation prescribed alongside ORS for children with diarrhea?

options.A: It sweetens the taste of ORS to make it easier to swallow
options.B: It acts as a mild sedative to help the sick child sleep
options.C: It reduces the duration and severity of the diarrhea episode and prevents recurrence for the next 2 to 3 months
options.D: It kills the bacterial pathogens directly in the stomach

explanation: Zinc is an essential micronutrient lost during diarrhea. Supplementing zinc (20mg daily for 10-14 days; 10mg for infants under 6 months) helps repair the intestinal mucosa, reduces the severity and duration of diarrhea, and boosts immunity to prevent subsequent episodes.

text: What is the protocol for administering Intermittent Preventive Treatment of malaria in pregnancy (IPTp) using Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine (SP)?

options.A: Daily doses starting from the first trimester until delivery
options.B: Single doses given at monthly intervals starting at quickening (second trimester), with at least 3 doses before delivery
options.C: Only given if the pregnant woman tests positive for malaria
options.D: Administered weekly in the third trimester only

explanation: WHO recommends IPTp-SP for all pregnant women in moderate-to-high malaria transmission areas. It is given as a DOT (Directly Observed Therapy) at each scheduled ANC visit starting at quickening (second trimester), at least 1 month apart, for a minimum of 3 doses.

text: What is the primary objective of conducting a community diagnosis in primary healthcare?

options.A: To prescribe individual clinical medications to all villagers
options.B: To identify the collective health status, problems, resources, and felt needs of the community to plan interventions
options.C: To punish community members who do not practice hygiene
options.D: To determine the budget requirements of the state hospital

explanation: Community diagnosis is a comprehensive profile of a community's health status, including environmental, social, and economic factors, as well as resources. This helps health workers prioritize health problems and design targeted community-based interventions.

text: How do the clinical presentations of Kwashiorkor and Marasmus differ?

options.A: Kwashiorkor presents with severe muscle wasting and no edema; Marasmus presents with bilateral pitting edema
options.B: Kwashiorkor presents with bilateral pitting edema, swollen belly, and skin/hair changes; Marasmus presents with severe muscle wasting and an 'old-man' face without edema
options.C: Kwashiorkor is caused by lack of vitamins; Marasmus is caused by lack of calcium
options.D: Kwashiorkor is only seen in adults; Marasmus is only seen in infants

explanation: Kwashiorkor (edematous malnutrition) is characterized by protein deficiency, leading to fluid retention (edema), skin lesions (flaky paint dermatosis), and sparse reddish hair. Marasmus is severe calorie deficiency leading to extreme wasting of fat and muscle, giving a wrinkled 'old-man' appearance.

text: What is the primary treatment objective for a casualty suffering from heat stroke?

options.A: To administer warm fluids immediately to prevent shivering
options.B: To rapidly lower the core body temperature using cooling techniques to prevent brain and organ damage
options.C: To administer oral pain relievers and antibiotics
options.D: To induce vomiting to clear potential toxins

explanation: Heat stroke is a life-threatening medical emergency where the body's temperature regulation mechanism fails (core temp > 40°C). The primary objective is to cool the body rapidly (using water spray, fan, ice packs in armpit/groin) to protect the brain and internal organs.

text: What is the primary mode of transmission of Vibrio cholerae?

options.A: Through the bite of infected tsetse flies
options.B: Inhalation of airborne dust particles
options.C: Fecal-oral route via ingestion of food or water contaminated with feces of an infected person
options.D: Direct contact with blood or body fluids of a patient

explanation: Cholera is transmitted via the fecal-oral route. This occurs when feces from an infected person contaminate drinking water reservoirs, well water, or food crops, which are subsequently ingested by others due to poor sanitation.

text: What does a visible permanent scar on the left upper arm of an infant following a BCG vaccine indicate?

options.A: An allergic reaction requiring antihistamine treatment
options.B: Successful intradermal vaccination and development of local cell-mediated immunity against tuberculosis
options.C: Poor injection technique by the health worker
options.D: The child has active pulmonary tuberculosis

explanation: The BCG vaccine normally causes a small red papule that forms an ulcer and heals over several weeks, leaving a small, flat scar. This scar indicates correct intradermal administration and normal immune response. Its absence does not necessarily mean the vaccine failed, but the scar is a positive indicator.

text: What is the purpose of establishing a Ward Development Committee (WDC) in the Primary Health Care system?

options.A: To act as a political campaign team for local ward counselors
options.B: To serve as a community-based governance body to promote community participation, ownership, and management of local health resources
options.C: To enforce legal fines on villagers who refuse vaccination
options.D: To distribute commercial pharmaceuticals for profit

explanation: The WDC is a key structure in PHC representing the community. It consists of local leaders, women, and youth representatives. It ensures community involvement in health decisions, assists in clinic maintenance, mobilization, and bridges the community-facility gap.

text: Which three criteria must be met for the Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM) to be highly effective as a family planning method?

options.A: Mother is breastfeeding once a day, baby is under 12 months, and menstrual periods have returned
options.B: Mother is exclusively breastfeeding (day and night), baby is under 6 months, and mother's menstrual periods have not returned
options.C: Mother is using formula milk, baby is under 3 months, and bleeding has stopped
options.D: Mother is pumping breast milk, baby is over 6 months, and mother is taking oral pills

explanation: LAM is a highly effective temporary family planning method. It works only if: 1. The mother's monthly bleeding has not returned. 2. The baby is exclusively breastfed (no other foods or liquids, fed on demand day and night). 3. The baby is less than 6 months old.

text: Which of the following represents a list of critical danger signs in pregnancy that require immediate referral to a comprehensive facility?

options.A: Mild morning sickness, frequent urination, and slight backache
options.B: Vaginal bleeding, severe headache with blurred vision, convulsions, high fever, and severe abdominal pain
options.C: Increased appetite, mild ankle swelling at the end of the day, and fatigue
options.D: Braxton Hicks contractions and breast enlargement

explanation: Critical danger signs indicate life-threatening complications (like placenta previa, pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, severe sepsis, or ectopic pregnancy). They require urgent clinical intervention and cannot be managed at lower-level PHC facilities.

text: Under IMCI guidelines, which clinical signs suggest neonatal sepsis in an infant under 2 months of age?

options.A: Frequent crying and passing soft stool twice a day
options.B: Poor feeding/sucking, lethargy or unconsciousness, convulsions, fast breathing (>= 60 breaths/min), and high or low temperature
options.C: Normal skin color and sleeping 16 hours a day
options.D: Mild physiological jaundice appearing on day 3

explanation: Young infants (under 2 months) have subtle signs of infection. IMCI lists signs of possible serious bacterial infection (sepsis) as: convulsion, fast breathing (>=60 breaths/min), severe chest indrawing, nasal flaring, grunting, high temperature (>37.5°C) or hypothermia (<35.5°C), poor feeding, or movement only when stimulated.

text: Why is colostrum (the first yellow breast milk produced after delivery) highly beneficial for the newborn?

options.A: It has high sugar content to keep the baby sleeping
options.B: It is rich in protein, Vitamin A, and maternal antibodies (especially IgA), acting as a natural vaccine and mild laxative
options.C: It is easier to digest because it contains no proteins
options.D: It prevents the baby from developing neonatal jaundice

explanation: Colostrum is thin, yellow, and concentrated. It contains high levels of immunoglobulins (antibodies, especially secretory IgA) that coat the baby's immature gut, protecting against pathogens. It also has a mild laxative effect that helps clear meconium.

text: What is the difference between an epidemic and an endemic disease?

options.A: An epidemic occurs globally; an endemic disease is restricted to monkeys
options.B: An epidemic is a sudden increase in cases of a disease above what is normally expected in a population; an endemic disease is constantly present at a baseline level in a geographic area
options.C: An epidemic is a disease that only affects children; an endemic disease affects adults
options.D: There is no difference; the terms are used interchangeably

explanation: Endemic refers to the constant presence or usual prevalence of a disease in a population or geographic area (e.g. malaria in Nigeria). Epidemic refers to an outbreak where cases suddenly spike far beyond normal baseline levels in a community or region.

text: What is meant by 'safe water chain' in environmental sanitation?

options.A: A system of pipes connecting a dam to the house
options.B: Ensuring water is protected from contamination at every step: source, transport, storage, and retrieval/handling
options.C: Adding chlorine tablets to water filters once a year
options.D: Using steel containers to carry water rather than plastic buckets

explanation: The safe water chain emphasizes that clean water at the source can easily become contaminated during transport (dirty containers), storage (open buckets), or retrieval (dipping dirty cups). All steps must remain clean and sealed to prevent diarrheal diseases.

text: Which of the following lists key modifiable risk factors for developing Type 2 Diabetes and Hypertension?

options.A: Genetics, blood type, and height
options.B: Unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, tobacco use, and harmful alcohol use
options.C: Air pollution and water hardness
options.D: Lack of routine vaccinations in childhood

explanation: Type 2 Diabetes and Hypertension are non-communicable lifestyle diseases. Modifiable risk factors are behaviors that individuals can change, including eating foods high in fat and salt, lack of exercise, smoking, and excessive drinking.

text: What is the correct first aid management for a casualty with a suspected venomous snakebite on the leg?

options.A: Cut the wound with a razor blade, suck out the venom, and apply a tight tourniquet
options.B: Keep the patient calm, immobilize the limb using a splint at or slightly below heart level, clean the wound, and transfer to a facility for antivenom
options.C: Apply ice directly to the bite and make the patient run to generate heat
options.D: Pour kerosene on the bite and squeeze the leg hard

explanation: Do not cut, suck, or apply tight tourniquets, as these increase local tissue damage, infection risk, and can cause systemic toxicity when released. Immobilization minimizes lymphatic spread of venom. Calmness slows heart rate, delaying systemic venom absorption.

text: What is the role of a Community Health Extension Worker (CHEW) in integrated disease surveillance?

options.A: To treat patients in high-end private hospitals
options.B: To monitor, identify, record, and immediately report cases of epidemic-prone diseases within the community and clinic, and participate in control measures
options.C: To develop new vaccines in laboratory settings
options.D: To quarantine whole villages without permission

explanation: CHEWs are the front line of surveillance. They use case definitions to detect reportable diseases (like cholera, measles, yellow fever) during clinic consultations and home visits, log them in registers, report to the LGA disease surveillance officer, and educate communities.

text: What four core symptoms are used to screen a patient for active tuberculosis in primary healthcare?

options.A: Diarrhea, vomiting, headache, and joint pain
options.B: Cough lasting 2 weeks or more, fever, night sweats, and unexplained weight loss
options.C: Skin rash, blood in urine, neck stiffness, and photophobia
options.D: Chest pain, swollen legs, high blood pressure, and dizziness

explanation: These four cardinal symptoms are highly sensitive for identifying individuals who may have active pulmonary tuberculosis. A patient presenting with any of these should be referred for sputum examination (GeneXpert or AFB microscopy).

text: What is the difference between WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) Category 1 and Category 4 for contraceptive use?

options.A: Category 1 means the method is too expensive; Category 4 is free
options.B: Category 1 represents no restriction for the use of the contraceptive method; Category 4 represents an unacceptable health risk where the method must not be used
options.C: Category 1 is only for teenagers; Category 4 is for postmenopausal women
options.D: Category 1 requires surgery; Category 4 is an oral medication

explanation: The WHO MEC categories guide safe prescribing. Category 1: A condition for which there is no restriction on the use of the contraceptive method. Category 4: A condition that represents an unacceptable health risk if the contraceptive method is used (e.g. estrogen-containing pills in a woman with history of deep vein thrombosis).

text: What is meant by 'involution of the uterus' in postpartum care?

options.A: The enlargement of the uterus during early pregnancy
options.B: The process by which the uterus returns to its normal non-pregnant size and position after childbirth
options.C: The abnormal tilt of the uterus causing pelvic pain
options.D: The surgical removal of the uterus due to severe hemorrhage

explanation: Uterine involution is the physiological process where the postpartum uterus contracts and shrinks back from about 1 kg immediately after delivery to its non-pregnant weight of ~60 g by 6 weeks postpartum, driven by uterine contractions.

text: How do Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) and Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) differ in terms of administration and immunization mechanism?

options.A: OPV is injected and contains live virus; IPV is oral and contains dead virus
options.B: OPV is administered orally (live attenuated virus, producing gut immunity); IPV is administered via intramuscular injection (inactivated virus, producing systemic blood immunity)
options.C: OPV is given at 9 months; IPV is given only at birth
options.D: OPV is for adults; IPV is for infants only

explanation: OPV is given as oral drops, replicating in the intestine to induce mucosal IgA antibodies (gut immunity), which prevents transmission. IPV is an injection of killed virus that stimulates blood IgG antibodies, preventing paralysis but not gut replication.

text: What is the primary design improvement of a Ventilated Improved Pit (VIP) latrine over a standard pit latrine?

options.A: It uses flushing water to clear waste
options.B: It has a vertical vent pipe with a fly-screen mesh at the top to draw away odors and trap flies in the pipe
options.C: It is built using expensive stainless steel components
options.D: It requires a mechanical pump to extract odor

explanation: The VIP latrine utilizes a vent pipe painted black to absorb heat, creating an updraft that sucks air from the pit and out the top, eliminating odor. The screen mesh at the top prevents flies from escaping; they are attracted to the light at the top of the pipe, enter it, and die of dehydration.

text: In the Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) framework, how quickly should immediately reportable diseases (e.g., cholera, measles, Lassa fever) be reported to the LGA level?

options.A: Within 24 hours of case detection
options.B: Within 1 week
options.C: At the end of the monthly reporting cycle
options.D: Only if a major outbreak occurs

explanation: Immediately reportable diseases are epidemic-prone or targeted for eradication. Case detection must trigger immediate notification (within 24 hours) via telephone, SMS, or IDSR Form 002 to enable rapid contact tracing and epidemic control.

text: What is the core premise of the Health Belief Model (HBM) used in health education?

options.A: People will change behavior only if they are paid to do so
options.B: A person's health behavior depends on their perception of susceptibility, severity of the illness, benefits of action, barriers, and cues to action
options.C: Health beliefs are entirely determined by genetic inheritance
options.D: Education has no influence on cultural beliefs

explanation: The Health Belief Model is a psychological health behavior model. It posits that people are likely to adopt a healthy behavior if they believe they are at risk (susceptibility), that the illness has serious consequences (severity), that the behavior works (benefits), and that they can overcome obstacles (barriers).

text: At what age should complementary feeding be introduced, and what are the essential attributes of complementary foods?

options.A: At 3 months; foods must be highly liquid and sugary
options.B: At 6 months; foods must be timely, adequate, safe, and appropriately fed in terms of texture and frequency
options.C: At 12 months; foods must contain only dairy products
options.D: At 9 months; foods should consist only of plain water and mashed yams

explanation: At 6 months, breast milk alone is no longer sufficient to meet the nutritional demands of the growing infant. Complementary feeding must begin: timely (at 6 months), adequate (providing energy, protein, micronutrients), safe (hygienically prepared), and appropriate (correct texture/portions).

text: What is the standard chest compression to ventilation ratio for performing Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) on an adult by a single rescuer?

options.A: 15 compressions to 2 ventilations
options.B: 30 compressions to 2 ventilations
options.C: 30 compressions to 5 ventilations
options.D: 10 compressions to 1 ventilation

explanation: For an adult casualty in cardiac arrest, a single rescuer (and dual rescuers) should perform cycles of 30 chest compressions (at a depth of 2-2.4 inches and rate of 100-120 compressions per minute) followed by 2 rescue breaths.

text: What are the three core components of Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) for low-birthweight and preterm infants?

options.A: Keeping the baby in an incubator, using formula milk, and strict visiting hours
options.B: Continuous skin-to-skin contact, exclusive breastfeeding, and early discharge from the facility with close follow-up
options.C: Injecting antibiotics daily, using cotton wraps, and feeding sugar water
options.D: Giving the infant warm baths, swaddling tightly, and separating from the mother

explanation: Kangaroo Mother Care is an evidence-based method for preterm/LBW infants. Its core features are: 1. Kangaroo position (continuous, prolonged skin-to-skin contact against the mother's chest). 2. Kangaroo nutrition (exclusive breastfeeding). 3. Early discharge with support and monitoring.
